variants.title: Admit inside the deadline
variants.context: Admission compares predicted completion against the caller's remaining budget. Validate the request, estimate queue, batch, execution, and response time, reserve memory and concurrency, then admit only when the predicted finish beats the deadline and the tenant budget allows it.
variants.prompt: An interactive ranking pool receives a request with a 180 ms deadline and enough warm capacity to serve it. Put the admission steps in order.

items.text: Estimate queue, batch, execution, and response time from the workload slice that matches this shape.
Reserve memory and concurrency for the model state and the per-request runtime buffers.
Admit the request because the predicted finish time lands before the deadline and the tenant budget allows it.
Validate the request and reject unsupported shapes, versions, or sizes before anything is queued.

variants.hint: Which check protects the accelerator before any capacity is committed?
variants.explanation: Validate, estimate, reserve, then test the deadline and the tenant budget. Capacity is committed only after the prediction says the work can finish.

variants.context: Admission compares predicted completion against the caller's remaining budget. Validate the request, estimate queue, batch, execution, and response time, reserve memory and concurrency, then admit only when the predicted finish beats the deadline and the tenant budget allows it.
variants.prompt: A burst pushes queue age up and a new request arrives with only 60 ms of deadline left. Put the admission steps in order, ending with what the controller does.

items.text: Defer the work to the asynchronous path and release the reservation instead of queueing it.
Reserve the memory and concurrency the request would need if it ran.
Validate the payload and confirm the requested model version is supported by this pool.
Compare the predicted finish time with the 60 ms that remains and find the request short.
Estimate the stage times from the burst workload slice rather than the calm-hour profile.

variants.hint: An unfinishable request still consumes the slot it waits in.
variants.explanation: Shedding early is cheaper than letting expired work occupy the accelerator while newer viable requests wait.

variants.title: Admit inside the deadline
variants.context: Admission compares predicted completion against the caller's remaining budget. Validate the request, estimate queue, batch, execution, and response time, reserve memory and concurrency, then admit only when the predicted finish beats the deadline and the tenant budget allows it.
variants.prompt: A tenant has exhausted its budget for the hour, but the fleet has warm capacity and the deadline is generous. Put the admission steps in order.

items.text: Estimate queue, batch, execution, and response time for that shape.
Find the tenant budget exhausted even though the predicted finish beats the deadline.
Route the request to the declared compatible fallback and record the decision reason.
Reserve queue, memory, and accelerator concurrency by priority class.
Validate the request shape, size, and requested capability name.

variants.hint: Two conditions gate admission, not one.
variants.explanation: The admit test is deadline and tenant budget together. When either fails, the answer is reject, defer, or a declared fallback.

variants.title: Drain a replica safely
variants.context: Shutdown is a designed path, not a signal handler afterthought. Mark the replica unavailable, stop admission and propagate cancellation, drain bounded in-flight work inside the termination budget, resolve stateful work by contract, and flush telemetry before releasing accelerator memory.
variants.prompt: A replica is being replaced during a routine version rollout. Put the shutdown steps in order.

items.text: Stop admission and propagate cancellation to requests still waiting in its queue.
Fail or hand off stateful work according to the contract that request class declared.
Flush telemetry before releasing accelerator memory and exiting.
Mark the replica unavailable so the router stops selecting it for new work.
Drain the bounded in-flight work that fits inside the termination budget.

variants.hint: What has to stop arriving before anything can finish draining?
variants.explanation: Readiness comes off first, then cancellation, then bounded drain. Telemetry is flushed before memory is released so the shutdown is explainable.

variants.title: Drain a replica safely
variants.context: Shutdown is a designed path, not a signal handler afterthought. Mark the replica unavailable, stop admission and propagate cancellation, drain bounded in-flight work inside the termination budget, resolve stateful work by contract, and flush telemetry before releasing accelerator memory.
variants.prompt: The autoscaler is scaling down after a burst and must keep a warm floor intact. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Hand the remaining stateful sequences to a compatible replica or fail them by contract.
Stop admission and cancel queued requests that have not started executing.
Finish the in-flight generations that can complete inside the termination budget.
Flush metrics and traces, then release accelerator memory and exit.
Remove readiness for this replica so the router stops choosing it while the rest of the fleet stays warm.

variants.hint: Scale-down is the same path as a rollout, only triggered by capacity.
variants.explanation: Deliberate drain protects the warm floor: new admission stops first, bounded work finishes, and stateful work is resolved before memory is released.

variants.title: Drain a replica safely
variants.context: Shutdown is a designed path, not a signal handler afterthought. Mark the replica unavailable, stop admission and propagate cancellation, drain bounded in-flight work inside the termination budget, resolve stateful work by contract, and flush telemetry before releasing accelerator memory.
variants.prompt: A node preemption gives the replica a 30 second termination budget. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Fail the rest with a retryable status that carries the original request identity.
Complete only the requests that can finish inside the 30 seconds that remain.
Flush telemetry, then release device memory and exit before the process is killed.
Propagate cancellation to queued requests rather than letting them wait out the budget.
Remove readiness immediately so the gateway routes no further requests here.

variants.hint: A short budget changes what you can finish, not the order.
variants.explanation: A short termination budget shrinks the drain window; it does not let you skip cancellation, identity-carrying failures, or the telemetry flush.

variants.title: Split the latency budget
variants.context: One deadline covers ingress, queue time, batch delay, execution, and response time together. A stage budget is whatever remains after the other stages have taken their share.
variants.prompt: A ranking service promises 180 ms end to end. Ingress takes 12 ms, queue time is 40 ms, the batch window contributes 8 ms, and the response gate plus serialization takes 15 ms. How many milliseconds remain for execution?
variants.hint: List every stage that spends the same deadline before you subtract.
variants.explanation: Execution gets what is left after ingress, queue, batch delay, and response time. A plan that ignores one stage misses the deadline in production.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts ingress and queue only; the batch window and response gate spend the same deadline.
That leaves out the response gate, which runs inside the deadline too.

variants.title: Split the latency budget
variants.context: One deadline covers ingress, queue time, batch delay, execution, and response time together. A stage budget is whatever remains after the other stages have taken their share.
variants.prompt: A streaming endpoint measures ingress 10 ms, queue 55 ms, batch delay 25 ms, execution 70 ms, and response 10 ms against a 150 ms deadline. By how many milliseconds does the measured path exceed the deadline?
variants.hint: Total every measured stage first, then compare it with the promise.
variants.explanation: Batch delay is real latency spent before execution starts, so it belongs in the total that the deadline has to cover.

mistakes.feedback: That is the total measured path, not the amount by which it overruns the deadline.
That drops the 25 ms batch window from the total, which is time genuinely spent before execution.

variants.title: Split the latency budget
variants.context: One deadline covers ingress, queue time, batch delay, execution, and response time together. A stage budget is whatever remains after the other stages have taken their share.
variants.prompt: A pool holds a 240 ms deadline. Ingress has already spent 18 ms, predicted batch delay is 12 ms, predicted execution is 96 ms, and the response gate needs 24 ms. What is the largest queue time admission may still allow, in milliseconds?
variants.hint: The queue gets the remainder, not the whole deadline.
variants.explanation: Admission has to reserve the downstream stages before it decides how long a request may wait, otherwise the queue silently spends the execution budget.

mistakes.feedback: That forgets the response gate, which is inside the same deadline.
That subtracts ingress only; batch delay, execution, and the response gate still need their share.

variants.title: Name the cache boundary
variants.context: A serving system runs several unrelated caches. The artifact cache holds immutable model files by digest, the resident model cache holds weights in accelerator memory, the feature cache holds reusable inputs, and the prediction cache holds reusable outputs. Each has its own key, invalidation rule, and security boundary.
variants.prompt: A serving team calls four different stores 'the cache' in one design review. Match each cache to what it actually holds and what its key must guarantee.

pairs.label: Artifact cache
pairs.detail: Immutable model files stored by digest, with integrity verified before a worker activates them.

pairs.label: Resident model cache
pairs.detail: Weights held in accelerator memory so a routed request can skip model-load latency.

pairs.label: Feature or embedding cache
pairs.detail: Reusable inputs keyed by source version, transformation version, authorization scope, and expiry.

pairs.label: Prediction cache
pairs.detail: Reusable outputs, safe only when the key covers model, adapter, decoding parameters, policy, and tenant.

variants.hint: Ask what the key must contain before you ask how fast the store is.
variants.explanation: Each cache has a different key, invalidation rule, and security boundary, so one shared label hides correctness bugs.

variants.title: Name the cache boundary
variants.context: A serving system runs several unrelated caches. The artifact cache holds immutable model files by digest, the resident model cache holds weights in accelerator memory, the feature cache holds reusable inputs, and the prediction cache holds reusable outputs. Each has its own key, invalidation rule, and security boundary.
variants.prompt: Four incidents land in the same week. Match each symptom to the cache boundary that produced it.

pairs.label: Answers look valid but reflect last week's account state
pairs.detail: A feature cache key missing the source version or an expiry

pairs.label: The first request for a rarely used model takes seconds
pairs.detail: A resident model cache miss forcing a cold model load

pairs.label: Two tenants receive the same response for the same normalized input
pairs.detail: A prediction cache key that omits the tenant boundary

pairs.label: A rollback activates a file that no longer matches the version manifest
pairs.detail: An artifact cache entry trusted from a mutable tag instead of a digest

variants.hint: Trace the symptom back to which key was too small.
variants.explanation: Stale features produce valid-looking but wrong predictions, and a missing key field turns a cache into a correctness bug rather than a speedup.

variants.title: Name the cache boundary
variants.context: A serving system runs several unrelated caches. The artifact cache holds immutable model files by digest, the resident model cache holds weights in accelerator memory, the feature cache holds reusable inputs, and the prediction cache holds reusable outputs. Each has its own key, invalidation rule, and security boundary.
variants.prompt: A release changes several things at once. Match each change to the reason cache reuse must stop.

pairs.label: A new adapter ships on the same base model
pairs.detail: The adapter changes the output, so cached predictions no longer match the request

pairs.label: Decoding switches from greedy to sampled
pairs.detail: Stochastic decoding makes a previous output unreusable for the same input

pairs.label: A tenant revokes consent for stored inputs
pairs.detail: Deletion obligations must reach cached copies, not only the source store

pairs.label: The response schema adds a required field
pairs.detail: Cached outputs no longer satisfy the response contract

variants.hint: Which of these changes the answer, and which changes who may see it?
variants.explanation: Never let cache reuse hide a version, boundary, decoding, schema, or deletion change; those are the exact cases where a hit returns the wrong answer fast.

variants.title: Diagnose the serving failure
variants.context: Serving failures show up before saturation does. Expired work in the queue, batch windows that hide tail latency, retries that multiply load, and readiness that reports warm before weights are usable all keep devices busy while users miss their deadlines.
variants.prompt: Accelerator utilization sits at 95 percent, yet a third of requests return deadline errors and queue age keeps climbing. What is actually happening?
options: Expired work occupies capacity while newer viable requests wait, so shed or defer before admitting it.
The batch window is too small, so widening it will bring latency back inside the deadline.
High utilization proves the fleet is healthy, so the published deadline should be relaxed.
optionFeedback: The queue became the product: requests wait past their deadline while devices stay busy on work nobody will use.
A wider window adds latency before execution, which makes deadline misses worse, not better.
Utilization measures busy devices, not useful completions; goodput is what the contract counts.
variants.hint: Busy devices and missed deadlines can be true at the same time.
variants.explanation: Measure goodput, not utilization. Work that will miss its deadline should be rejected or deferred before it consumes an accelerator slot.

variants.title: Diagnose the serving failure
variants.context: Serving failures show up before saturation does. Expired work in the queue, batch windows that hide tail latency, retries that multiply load, and readiness that reports warm before weights are usable all keep devices busy while users miss their deadlines.
variants.prompt: After the batch window was doubled, average throughput rose but p99 latency for long inputs got much worse. What should the team conclude?
options: Batching is hiding tail latency, so cap batch delay and track queue age by shape bucket.
The checkpoint regressed with the release, so roll the model version back first.
The fleet is under-provisioned, so add replicas until the p99 number recovers.
optionFeedback: Sparse and large requests wait behind preferred shapes while the average improves.
Nothing about the model changed; the scheduler's waiting policy did.
More replicas do not remove a batch delay that every request pays before execution.
variants.hint: Which requests pay for an average that improved?
variants.explanation: Track queue age and latency by shape bucket, and cap batch delay, because a throughput average can rise while a whole class of requests misses its deadline.

variants.title: Diagnose the serving failure
variants.context: Serving failures show up before saturation does. Expired work in the queue, batch windows that hide tail latency, retries that multiply load, and readiness that reports warm before weights are usable all keep devices busy while users miss their deadlines.
variants.prompt: A predictable morning burst arrives. The autoscaler adds replicas quickly, they report ready within seconds, and errors continue for several minutes while the new workers return slow first responses.
options: The liveness probe is too aggressive, so lengthen its interval to stop restarts during load.
The utilization target is too high, so lower it and let the autoscaler add replicas sooner.
Readiness lied about warmth, so make it model-version aware and run a bounded warm-up before routing.
optionFeedback: Nothing here restarted; the replicas accepted traffic they could not serve yet.
Earlier scaling still routes traffic to replicas that report ready before they are warm.
The port opened before weights, runtime memory, and adapters were usable, so traffic reached cold workers.
variants.hint: A scheduled process is not serving capacity yet.
variants.explanation: Readiness must prove a specific model and version is loaded and warmed. Otherwise autoscaling adds replicas that accept traffic they cannot serve.
